new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (116 pp., ANU open-access bitstream). extracted text of PDF p. 24 = book p. 368 and the saved page image both show section 2.6.2.2.5.2 'Kaygir' with the sentence 'In bi-syllabic words the final syllable is stressed.' immediately after the phoneme list. The reader's quote is verbatim except that it replaces the r allophones '[r̃, r̆]' with '[..]'; everything else (including 'Tamagário', 'and perhaps ə') matches the page image. Surrounding section read: 2.6.2.2.5.0 (pp. 366-367) introduces the Kayagar stock-level family (Kaugat ~700, Kaygir ~3,000, Tamagario ~3,500 speakers; Gondu and Cook river basins; 'the dialect situation in Kaygir is not known'; only published materials = Voorhoev…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In disyllabic words primary stress falls on the last syllable. Nothing is said about longer words; the same one-line rule is given for the sister languages Tamagario (explicitly 'non-tonal') and Kaugat on pp. 367-368, so the whole Kayagar family is described as word-final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Voorhoeve 1971 p. 85 adds that in word-final clusters /pm/ and /tn/ the nasal is syllabic and 'can carry stress [pm̩, tn̩]'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms from elicited wordlists (Voorhoeve's 1970 field trip; two Kajgir wordlists from Kawem village). The rule covers bisyllabic words only; 'Further grammatical information is lacking.' Short survey-chapter sketch, not a full phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve names the language 'Kaygir' (1975) / 'Kajgir', 'Kaigir' (1971); Glottolog lists Kaygir as an alternative name of Kayagar [kyt] (kaya1328), and Kriens et al. 2011 confirm Voorhoeve's 1971 village list is the Kayagar village list. Voorhoeve's data come from Kawem village (upper Cook / Peru / lower Gondu rivers), i.e. the western 'Wiyagar' dialect area; the 'dialect situation in Kaygir is not known' (1975 p. 367). The same page pair (pp. 367-368) gives identical final-stress statements for Tamagario (tama1336) and Kaugat (= Atohwaim, atoh1238), the two other Kayagaric languages currently marked no source found.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page for Kayagar (kaya1328) and reference record 105050 (Kriens et al. 2011).
sources.note: Lists only Voorhoeve 1971 (pp. 87-88, subclassification comment) and Ethnologue 2025 for the language; the earlier target record lists 8 overview/wordlist refs and 0 descriptive refs. Alternative names: Kajagar, Kajakaja, Kayagi, Kaygir, Wiyagar.
No phonology at all; cites Ethnologue, Kriens et al. 2011 and a 1961 Dutch patrol report (Krosschell). Gives dialects Wiyagar (Assue District) and Kaigar (Amagais, Asmat Regency).

sources.note: Sociolinguistic survey (May 2002) of 7 Kayagar villages; finds two dialects ('Wiyagar': Okor, Atsipim, Tsemtaipim, Warogom, Gairipim; 'Tamario': Arare, Pagai). No statement on stress; the lexicostatistic rules (Appendix E, PDF p. 44) say 'Unreleased consonants, accents, and nasalized vowels are ignored.' The Appendix F/G phonetic wordlists do carry IPA stress marks (e.g. foˈɣum 'hit', tau̯ˈte 'bite', takʰaˈren 'why'), i.e. raw primary data but no rule. downloaded from the the Internet Archive because sil.org blocks automated downloads.

sources.note: Section 3.2 'The Kajagar Family' (pp. 80-88) gives consonant and vowel phoneme charts for Kaugat, Kaigir (= Kayagar) and Tamagario but no general stress rule; the only stress remark is p. 85 (section 3.2.2.3 Distribution, verified on page image): word-final clusters /pm/ and /tn/ contrast with final /p/ and /t/ and 'the nasal in these clusters can carry stress [pm̩, tn̩]'. Appendix II comparative wordlist (Kaugat, Kajgir, Tamagario, Sawuj..) carries no stress marks. Mentions that Father F. Lommertsen M.S.C. lent the author manuscript grammatical sketches of Kajgir and Joggo (p. 82).
